ev-sarj-cihazi-modelleri-karsilastirma.title: EV Charger Models Compared: Which One Is Right for You?
ev-sarj-cihazi-modelleri-karsilastirma.description: Compare AC wallbox, DC fast charging and portable electric vehicle charger models by power, phase, connector and smart features — and choose the right one for you, step by step.
ev-sarj-cihazi-modelleri-karsilastirma.excerpt: Which charger for home, work or public use? A buyer's guide that compares AC wallbox, DC and portable models by power, phase and OCPP, complete with decision tables.

body.text: The question most people ask when choosing an electric vehicle charger is: with so many models out there, which one is right for me? The honest answer isn't a single model — it's hidden in your usage scenario. Will you charge at home, at work or at a public point? Is your electrical supply single-phase or three-phase? Is speed your priority, or portability? In this guide we compare AC wallbox, DC fast charging and portable models using their real technical figures, and explain exactly which to choose in each situation with clear tables.
First decision: AC, DC or portable?
Before picking a model, you need to settle on the charging type. There are three main groups, and for most people the choice becomes clear quickly:

items: AC Wallbox (wall-mounted): the standard solution for homes, apartment blocks and workplaces. It charges at 3.7–22 kW through the car's own onboard charger and is ideal for overnight or all-day charging.

DC Fast Charging: for public points, motorways, shopping centres and fleets. It fills the car far faster at 40 kW and above, but requires high-power three-phase infrastructure and isn't installed at home.
Portable Charger: a flexible, plug-in solution you carry with you — suitable as a second/backup charger or for anyone who can't fit a fixed unit.

body.text: AC wallbox models compared

The Bemis AC wallbox range is fully Type 2 (IEC 62196-2) and goes up to 22 kW on three-phase infrastructure. The range extends from an entry-level model up to a smart/connected model, and every model is available with a fixed 5-metre cable or a panel-socket output.

body.caption: Bemis AC Wallbox models — technical comparison

body.text: Charger 2 is the entry level, with a fixed 11/22 kW. Charger Plus 2 and Charger Pro 2 let you adjust the power between 4/7/11/22 kW (you can dial it down to your installation's limit). Charger Pro 2 GSM, with its GSM module and OCPP 1.6 protocol, is built for workplace and fleet scenarios that need remote management, user authorisation and reporting.
DC fast charging models compared

The Bemis DC range (BEVDC) is designed for public and fleet use; every unit takes an AC 380–480V 3-phase input, delivers a 150–1000V DC output through a CCS2 connector and is OCPP 1.6J / 2.0.1 compatible. Power and the number of sockets are chosen to suit the need:

body.caption: Bemis DC fast charging models — technical comparison

body.text: The single-socket, lower-power models (BEVDC 40) suit small businesses and single-point scenarios; the dual-socket, higher-power models capable of simultaneous charging (80 kW and above) are suited to busy stations and motorway locations.
Portable charger models

The portable range consists of flexible, plug-in solutions that come with their own carry case and need no fixed installation. There are three tiers to match your power needs and your electrical supply (single-phase/three-phase):

body.caption: Bemis portable charger models

body.text: Mini Mobile is the most compact option for a household socket and emergency/backup use. Mono Mobile delivers higher power on a single-phase supply and comes with socket adapters. Pro Mobile goes up to 22 kW on a three-phase supply — it's for those who want power close to a wallbox despite the portability.
Fixed cable or panel socket?

The second decision you'll often face with AC models is the output type. On a cable model, the 5-metre Type 2 cable is fixed to the unit — you just plug in and charge, which is practical. On a panel-socket model, the unit has a Type 2 socket and you plug in your own cable; this suits users who run more than one car/cable or prefer to store the cable separately. Both deliver the same power; the difference comes down to how you like to use it.
Which model for which scenario?

items: Home / apartment (single car, overnight charging): AC Wallbox Charger 2, or the adjustable-power Charger Plus 2 — 7–11 kW is more than enough overnight for most cars.
Workplace / fleet (authorisation, reporting, payment): Charger Pro 2 GSM — remote management and per-user reporting via OCPP 1.6.
Public / motorway / shopping centre (speed matters): the DC range — BEVDC 40 (single point) or a dual-socket 80–200 kW unit, depending on traffic.
Travel / backup / where installation isn't possible: the portable range — Mini/Mono Mobile for single-phase, Pro Mobile for three-phase power.

body.text: Explore every Bemis EV charging model with its technical specs — all locally manufactured.
body.label: Explore Products

body.text: Whichever model you choose, Bemis E-V Charge products are manufactured locally at the company's integrated facilities in Bursa; the software and PCB design belong to Bemis. To choose the right model, remember to factor in your car's onboard charging power and the capacity of your electrical installation — and if you're not sure, we can work it out together at the quotation stage.

faq.q: How many kW of charger is enough for a home?
faq.a: For most home users, an AC wallbox in the 7–11 kW range is more than enough. While your car sits parked overnight for 8–10 hours, even 7.4 kW fully charges most batteries. Higher power (22 kW) only makes sense if you have a three-phase installation and your car's onboard charger accepts that power; otherwise the car itself is the limit. Because Bemis Charger Plus and Pro models let you adjust the power between 4/7/11/22 kW, you can pick the value that suits your installation and use it with confidence. When deciding, weigh up both your fuse/line capacity and your car's acceptance power together.

faq.q: Should I buy a cable model or a panel-socket model?
faq.a: Both deliver the same power; the difference comes down to how you like to use it. On a cable model, the 5-metre Type 2 cable is fixed to the unit — you arrive home, plug in and charge, which is the most practical method and ideal for most single-car home use. On a panel-socket model, the unit has a Type 2 socket and you plug in your own cable; this suits users who run more than one car, prefer to keep the cable in the boot, or want to store it separately. Panel-socket models can also be preferable at workplaces where different users bring their own cables.

faq.q: Can a DC fast charger be installed at home?
faq.a: In practice, no. DC fast chargers (the BEVDC range) operate at 40 kW and above, require a high-power AC 380–480V three-phase input, and are designed for public points, motorways, shopping centres and fleet depots. A home's standard electrical infrastructure can't supply this power, and an investment on this scale is unnecessary for home use. The right solution for home charging is an AC wallbox — at 7–11 kW it charges your car quietly and safely overnight. DC fast charging is positioned at public stations to meet the need for a quick top-up during a short stop on a long journey.

faq.q: When is smart charging (OCPP) necessary?
faq.a: OCPP (Open Charge Point Protocol) is an open standard that connects a charger to a management system, and it's generally needed in workplace, residential-complex and fleet scenarios. If you want to authorise users (via RFID/app), report the energy each user consumes, apply billing, or centrally monitor several units, an OCPP-compatible model is essential. The Bemis Charger Pro 2 GSM model meets these needs with its GSM module and OCPP 1.6 protocol. For single-car home use, OCPP isn't required; a simple wallbox is enough. If your needs are likely to grow, choosing an OCPP-compatible model from the outset makes the transition easier.

faq.q: Does a portable charger replace a fixed wallbox?
faq.a: Partly — it depends on the need. A portable charger (Mini/Mono/Pro Mobile) is a flexible solution you plug in and carry with you; it's ideal for users who can't fit a fixed unit, are renting, or want a second/backup charger. Pro Mobile comes close to a wallbox in power terms, reaching up to 22 kW on a three-phase installation. That said, a fixed wallbox — with its dedicated line, permanent mounting and generally more settled cable management — is more comfortable and durable for everyday home charging. If you'll charge regularly at one point, a wallbox makes sense; for mobile/flexible use, a portable charger does; and many users run both together.

elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-disarida-ya.title: Can You Use an EV Charging Cable Outdoors and in the Rain?
elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-disarida-ya.metaTitle: Can a Charging Cable Be Used in the Rain? (IP)
elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-disarida-ya.description: Can an electric vehicle charging cable and unit be used safely outdoors, in the rain? What do IP65/IP66 protection ratings mean, and what should you watch out for — a plain-English safety guide.
elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-disarida-ya.excerpt: Is it safe to charge your car in an open car park or in the rain? Outdoor use of charging cables and units, IP protection ratings and safety tips.

body.text: One of the questions new electric vehicle owners ask most often is: is it safe to charge my car in an open car park or in the rain? The short answer is yes — because electric vehicle charging equipment is built for outdoor conditions from the outset. But the detail lies in the protection rating of the unit and the cable. In this guide we explain what to watch out for.
Short answer: yes, safe with the right IP protection

Electric vehicle charging is already done largely outdoors (in home gardens, open car parks, roadside stations). That's why chargers, cables and Type 2 connectors are built to be protected against water and dust. The key is that the equipment's 'IP protection rating' is adequate.
What is an IP protection rating?

An IP protection rating is shown by the two digits that follow the letters 'IP'. The first digit indicates resistance to dust, the second to water. On electric vehicle equipment, you'll most often see these values:

items: IP54: largely protected against dust, and protected against splashing water — light conditions.
IP65: dust-tight + protected against water jets from any direction.
IP66: dust-tight + protected against powerful water jets — ideal for outdoors.

body.text: If you're doing a fixed installation in an open car park or a spot exposed to rainfall, choose a unit rated IP65 or higher. Bemis units and cables are manufactured CE-certified and with IP protection.
Tips for safe outdoor use

items: Keep the connector's cap closed when you're not using it; don't leave it on the ground.
Don't use a wet or damaged cable/connector; replace it if there are cracks, cuts or crushing.
Keep the contact surface as dry as possible when plugging the connector into the car.
Position the cable so it won't be crushed under a door, wheel or sharp edge.
Have the installation (particularly a fixed unit) done by a qualified electrician, with earthing and residual-current protection.

body.text: Explore Bemis CE-certified, IP-protected Type 2 charging cables.
body.label: Explore Charging Cables

faq.q: Can an electric vehicle charging cable be used in the rain?
faq.a: Yes. Electric vehicle charging cables and connectors are built for outdoor conditions from the outset, protected against water and dust, because most charging is done outdoors anyway. The key to safe use is that the equipment's IP protection rating is adequate — IP65 or higher is recommended for outdoors. When charging in the rain, it's good practice to keep the connector's contact surface as dry as possible, keep the cap closed on the connector when it's not in use, and never use a damaged cable. Follow these rules and charging in wet weather is safe.

faq.q: What is the difference between IP65 and IP66?
faq.a: Because the first digit of both is 6, both are fully dust-tight; the difference emerges in the second digit — that is, resistance to water. IP65 provides protection against low-pressure water jets from any direction. IP66 withstands stronger, high-pressure water jets. In practice, both are suitable for open car parks and rainy conditions; IP66 offers an extra safety margin for tougher environments (for example, frequently washed areas or regions with heavy rainfall). For outdoor electric vehicle installations, IP65 is sufficient in most cases, while IP66 is preferred by those who want top-tier protection.

faq.q: Is a charger waterproof?
faq.a: An electric vehicle charger with the appropriate IP protection rating is protected against water under normal operating conditions and won't let water in during rain, splashing and similar situations. For example, an IP65-rated unit is dust-tight and withstands water jets from any direction. However, no unit is 'submersible'; you should avoid extreme conditions such as flooding, immersion in standing water or pressure washing. The unit's covers and seals must be intact, and the cable entries must be installed with proper sealing. Bemis units are manufactured CE-certified and with IP protection; even so, having the installation done by a qualified electrician is important for the integrity of that protection.

faq.q: Can a fixed charging unit be installed in an open car park?
faq.a: Yes, a fixed charging unit (wallbox) can be installed in open car parks; this is a very common use. What matters is choosing a unit with an IP protection rating suitable for outdoors (ideally IP65 or higher) and installing it correctly. The installation requires a dedicated line, appropriate cable cross-section, a residual-current device and proper earthing — all of which must be planned by a qualified electrician. Where the unit is directly exposed to sun and rainfall, a small canopy extends its life but isn't mandatory. In residential-complex or shared car parks, management permission and the metering arrangement must also be planned in advance.

ev-sarj-unitesi-mi-tasinabilir-sarj-ciha.title: Home Charging Unit or Portable Charger? Which Is Right for You?
ev-sarj-unitesi-mi-tasinabilir-sarj-ciha.metaTitle: Home Charging Unit or Portable Charger?
ev-sarj-unitesi-mi-tasinabilir-sarj-ciha.description: For charging your electric vehicle at home, should you buy a wallbox (home charging unit) or a portable charger? A plain-English decision guide covering the differences in power, installation and use.
ev-sarj-unitesi-mi-tasinabilir-sarj-ciha.excerpt: There are two ways to charge at home: a wall-mounted home charging unit (wallbox) or a plug-in portable charger. Which is right for you? Their differences and a decision guide.

body.text: There are two basic ways to charge your electric car at home: a home charging unit (wallbox) fixed to the wall, or a portable charger you plug in and use. Both charge your car, but they differ in use, speed and installation. In this guide we clarify which one is right for you.
What is a home charging unit (wallbox)?

A wallbox is a fixed charging unit mounted on a garage or car-park wall and fed from its own electrical line. An electrician handles the installation. Thanks to the dedicated line it delivers higher, steadier power — up to 7.4 kW on a single-phase installation and up to 22 kW on a three-phase installation.

items: Faster, steadier charging (dedicated line).
The convenience of plug-and-charge every time you get home.
Features such as app control, RFID, OCPP and load management on smart models.
A fixed, tidy appearance — no cable clutter.

body.text: What is a portable charger?

A portable charger is a device you plug into an existing socket (a household Schuko socket or an industrial CEE socket) and carry with you. It needs no installation; you take it out of its case and plug it in. Power is generally lower on a Schuko socket (around 2.3–3.7 kW); it can go higher on a suitable CEE socket.

items: No installation — plugs into any suitable socket.
Portable: with you when travelling, at the summer house or visiting.
Also useful as a backup for a wallbox.
Generally a more affordable entry-level solution.

body.text: The main differences between the two

items: Power/speed: a wallbox is generally higher and steadier; a portable charger plugged into a Schuko socket is slower.
Installation: a wallbox needs an electrician + a dedicated line; a portable charger is plug-and-go.
Portability: a portable charger goes with you; a wallbox is fixed.
Smart features: app/OCPP/load management are generally stronger on the wallbox side.

body.text: Which one should you choose?

items: If you charge at home every day and want the fastest, tidiest solution → a home charging unit (wallbox).
If you want to get started without dealing with installation, carry the device with you, or have a backup → a portable charger.
The ideal scenario: keep both — a wallbox at home plus a portable charger as a backup in the car.

body.text: Bemis home charging units (AC Wallbox) and portable chargers are locally manufactured — compare the models.
body.label: Explore Home Charging Units

faq.q: What is a home charging unit (wallbox)?
faq.a: A home charging unit, commonly known as a wallbox, is a fixed charger mounted on a garage or car-park wall and fed from its own electrical line. An electrician handles the installation, and thanks to the dedicated line it delivers high, steady power: up to 7.4 kW on a single-phase installation and up to 22 kW on a three-phase installation. It lets you plug in and charge every time you get home; smart models offer features such as app control, RFID authorisation, OCPP compatibility and load management that balances several units. With its fixed, tidy appearance, it's the most practical solution for everyday home use.

faq.q: Is a portable charger suitable for daily home use?
faq.a: Yes, a portable charger works comfortably for everyday home use; it's enough to charge your car overnight, especially if your daily mileage is low. A big advantage is that it needs no installation: you plug it into a suitable socket and use it. However, power is generally lower on a standard household Schuko socket (around 2.3–3.7 kW), so charging is slower. If you have high daily mileage or want to fill the car quickly, a fixed home charging unit (wallbox) is more suitable. Many users run a wallbox at home and keep a portable charger with them for travel and backup.

faq.q: Does a home charging unit charge faster?
faq.a: Generally, yes. Because a home charging unit (wallbox) is fed from its own dedicated electrical line, it delivers higher, steadier power — up to 7.4 kW on a single-phase installation and up to 22 kW on a three-phase installation. A portable charger plugged into a standard Schuko socket generally stays around 2.3–3.7 kW, so it charges more slowly. Even so, the real charging speed is also limited by the AC charging unit inside your car (the onboard charger); if your car accepts low-power AC, the gap between the two methods narrows. If speed is your priority, a wallbox is more advantageous.

faq.q: What is needed for a wallbox installation?
faq.a: A wallbox installation generally requires a dedicated (separate) line run from your electrical panel, a cable of the appropriate cross-section, and the correct protective devices (a residual-current device and a fuse). For a three-phase 22 kW installation, your installation must be three-phase; on a single-phase installation, power is limited to 7.4 kW. Always have the installation done by a qualified electrician; choosing the right line and protection is important for both safety and the unit's correct operation. If it's being installed in an apartment or residential-complex car park, permission from the management and the shared-meter/individual-meter arrangement must also be planned.

elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-kac-metre-k.title: How Many Metres and How Many Amps Should an EV Charging Cable Be?
elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-kac-metre-k.metaTitle: Charging Cable: How Many Metres, How Many Amps?
elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-kac-metre-k.description: When choosing an electric vehicle charging cable, how many amps (16A/32A) and how many metres (5–10 m) do you need? The single-phase/three-phase difference and the right cable for your car — a plain-English buyer's guide.
elektrikli-arac-sarj-kablosu-kac-metre-k.excerpt: The two questions most often asked when buying a charging cable: how many amps, and how many metres? A practical guide to choosing the right cable based on your car's power and your parking distance.

body.text: The two questions most often asked when buying an electric vehicle charging cable: how many amps (how many kW) and how many metres? The right answer depends on the charging power your car can accept and where you park it. In this guide we clarify both with examples.
Short answer

items: For most home users: a 32A, 5–7 metre Type 2 cable is ideal.
If your home is single-phase, 32A gives you up to 7.4 kW of charging.
If your home/workplace is three-phase and your car supports it, 22 kW is possible with 32A.
If the car parks close to the socket, 5 metres is enough; if the socket is far, choose 7–10 metres.

body.text: How many amps should it be? (16A or 32A?)
The amperage determines the current the cable can carry — that is, the charging power. There are two common values: 16A and 32A. The corresponding power figures by number of phases are as follows:

items: Single-phase (~230V): 16A ≈ 3.7 kW · 32A ≈ 7.4 kW
Three-phase (~400V): 16A ≈ 11 kW · 32A ≈ 22 kW

body.text: But no matter how powerful the cable, the real charging speed is limited by the AC charging unit inside your car (the onboard charger). For example, if your car accepts a maximum of 11 kW AC, it will charge at 11 kW even with a 22 kW cable. So the real question is: 'how many kW of AC charging does my car accept?' If you're not sure, a 32A cable is the safe choice; it's enough for both your current and your future car.
How many metres should it be?
Length is entirely a matter of practicality. The standard options are 5, 7 and 10 metres:

items: 5 metres: enough if you park close to the charging unit/socket; the most compact and affordable.
7 metres: the most balanced choice — a comfortable distance for most garage and car-park layouts.
10 metres: if the socket is far away, if you park the car facing the other way, or if you want flexibility in a shared car park.

body.text: Buying a longer cable than you need does no harm, but it's heavier, more expensive and more of a hassle to coil up. One or two metres more than you need makes an ideal buffer.
Single-phase or three-phase?

This depends on both your car and your electrical installation. Most homes have single-phase electricity; in that case you get a maximum of 7.4 kW (32A). At a workplace, residential-complex car park or a home with a three-phase supply, if three-phase is available and your car supports it, you can go up to 22 kW. Before choosing a cable, it's best to have an electrician confirm how many phases your installation has.
Summary: choose the right cable in 3 questions

items: How many kW of AC charging does my car accept? → this determines the amperage you need (32A is generally safe).
Is my installation single-phase or three-phase? → this sets the ceiling: single-phase 7.4 kW / three-phase 22 kW.
How far do I park my car from the socket? → 5, 7 or 10 metres.

body.text: Bemis Type 2 charging cables are locally manufactured, with 16A/32A, single-phase and three-phase, and 5–10 metre options.
body.label: Explore Charging Cables

faq.q: How many amps should an electric vehicle charging cable be?
faq.a: The two most common values are 16A and 32A. On a single-phase installation, 16A delivers about 3.7 kW and 32A about 7.4 kW; on a three-phase installation, 16A reaches about 11 kW and 32A about 22 kW. However, no matter how powerful the cable, the real charging speed is limited by the AC charging unit inside your car (the onboard charger). So first check how many kW of AC charging your car accepts. If you're not sure, a 32A cable is the safe choice; it offers enough capacity for both your current and your future car, and it works without issue on lower-power cars too.

faq.q: Is a 5-metre charging cable enough?
faq.a: If you park your car close to the charging unit or socket, 5 metres is enough for most home use; it's the most compact and affordable option. However, if the socket is in a far corner of the garage, if you sometimes park the car facing the other way, or if you want flexibility in a shared car park, 7 metres is the most balanced choice. If the socket really is far away, choose 10 metres. The general rule: add a 1–2 metre buffer to the distance you need. A longer cable than necessary works, but it's heavier, more expensive and more of a hassle to coil up.

faq.q: What is the difference between a 16A and a 32A charging cable?
faq.a: The difference is in the current the cable can carry and therefore the charging power. A 32A cable carries roughly twice the power of a 16A one: on a single-phase installation 16A ≈ 3.7 kW while 32A ≈ 7.4 kW; on a three-phase installation 16A ≈ 11 kW while 32A ≈ 22 kW. In other words, a 32A cable offers the potential to charge your car in less time. But to realise that potential, both your installation and your car must support that power. If your car is lower-powered, a 32A cable still works — it simply charges at the car's limit.

faq.q: Can a three-phase cable be used on a single-phase car?
faq.a: Yes, it can. The Type 2 connector is the same for both single-phase and three-phase, so there's no physical incompatibility when a three-phase cable is plugged into a single-phase car or a single-phase installation. In that case, charging takes place at the lowest capacity in the system: if your car or your installation is single-phase, power stays limited to 7.4 kW (32A), and the cable being three-phase brings no extra speed. So a three-phase cable is a safe, future-proof investment; if you later move to a three-phase installation or car, you can carry on using the same cable.

elektrikli-arac-sarj-istasyonu-kurulum-r.title: EV Charging Station Installation Guide
elektrikli-arac-sarj-istasyonu-kurulum-r.description: A step-by-step EV charging station installation guide: planning, required permits, electrical infrastructure, cable sizing, device selection, load management and commissioning.
elektrikli-arac-sarj-istasyonu-kurulum-r.excerpt: How do you install an EV charging station at home, in an apartment complex or at a business? From planning and permits to infrastructure, device selection and commissioning, we've gathered every step in one guide.

body.text: Once you switch to an electric vehicle, the biggest question is where and how you'll charge it. The most practical and economical approach is to charge at home, in your building or at work using your own charging station. But it isn't as simple as bolting an AC wallbox to the wall and plugging in: it takes proper planning, suitable electrical infrastructure, the necessary permits and a qualified installation. In this guide we bring home, apartment/building and workplace installations together in one place, laying out every step you need to know in plain terms so the whole process goes smoothly from start to finish.
What should you plan before installation begins?

A good installation begins at the desk, before a single cable is run. First, decide where you park your vehicle and where the charging device will be mounted; the distance between that point and the electrical panel directly affects the length and cost of the cable to be run. Next, find out your vehicle's onboard AC charging capacity: whatever the maximum AC power your car accepts, the charging speed will be capped at that limit no matter how powerful a device you install.
The key decisions to make during the planning stage are:

items: Installation location: detached garage, apartment/building car park or workplace car park (each requires different permits and infrastructure).
Target power: a value compatible with what the vehicle accepts and with the electrical capacity of the home or business (in the 7.4–22 kW AC range).
Single-phase or three-phase: if your installation is single-phase the typical ceiling is 7.4 kW; with three-phase you can reach 11–22 kW.
Cable route and distance: the distance between the panel and the device determines the cable cross-section and labour cost.
Future needs: if a second vehicle or a second point will be added later, designing the infrastructure for that from the outset is the most economical route.

body.text: Which permits do you need to install a charging station?

If you're installing in a garage on your own property in a detached house, you generally won't need any additional permission; the decision is entirely yours. Installing in a shared space such as an apartment or building car park is different: because it involves alterations and additional wiring in a common area, you first need to consult the building management or the property owners and obtain the necessary approval. In Turkey, the regulations are evolving to make electric vehicle charging infrastructure requests easier; even so, the best course is to speak with your building management and a qualified electrician to clarify the current, binding situation.

The second key point is the distribution (grid) side. For a single, low-power home installation, the existing subscription is usually sufficient. But with high-power or multi-point installations, total demand may exceed your existing subscription capacity; in that case a power upgrade or grid opinion from the electricity distribution company may be required. Your qualified electrician makes this assessment and, if needed, explains the process to be handled with the distribution company.
General rule: Your own garage is yours; the decision on a common area rests with building management, and grid capacity with the distribution company. Clarify permits before installation.
What kind of electrical infrastructure does a charging station require?

So it can operate independently of the rest of the home, the charging device should be fed as far as possible from a dedicated line run from the electrical panel. This line forms its own circuit at the panel with a device-specific fuse and protection; that way there's no conflict with the home's other loads during charging and safety improves. The capacity of the existing installation — that is, the main fuse and existing wiring — must be assessed against the continuous load the device will draw.
Why does cable cross-section matter?

Cable cross-section is the most critical factor determining the current a cable can carry safely without overheating. A charging device draws high, continuous current over long periods; a cable with an inadequate cross-section will overheat under this load, lose efficiency and create a safety risk. The correct cross-section is determined by the device's power (its ampere rating), whether it's single- or three-phase, and the distance between the panel and the device. As distance increases, a thicker cable is usually needed to compensate for voltage drop. This calculation must be done with precise figures by a qualified electrician; choosing a cable by guesswork is not the right approach.
Is residual current protection (RCD) mandatory?

Yes. A suitable residual current device (RCD) must be present on the line feeding the charging device. In the event of a leakage current or insulation fault, the RCD instantly cuts the circuit, providing protection against the risk of electric shock. Because EV charging is a continuous, high-current use, this protection is far more critical than for a standard household socket. Even if the device has its own internal safety functions, the correct type of residual current and overcurrent protection on the panel side is an indispensable part of the installation.

items: A dedicated supply line for the device, separate from the panel.
A cable cross-section correctly calculated for the power and distance.
The appropriate type of residual current protection (RCD) and overcurrent protection (fuse).
If required, a separate meter for the device (especially to separate consumption in a common area).
Solid earthing that complies with the standards.

body.text: Which charging device should I choose?

In the vast majority of home, building and workplace installations, the preferred device type is the AC wallbox. Where the vehicle is parked for long stretches (at home overnight, at work during the day), AC charging is both sufficient and gentle on the battery. In terms of power, single-phase installations typically use 7.4 kW models, while three-phase installations use models in the 11–22 kW range. When choosing a device, assess your vehicle's accepted power and your installation's capacity together; a device more powerful than needed provides no benefit if your vehicle can't draw that power.
The key features to consider when choosing an AC wallbox:

items: Connector: Type 2, the Turkish and European standard (compatible with all modern electric vehicles).
Power and phase: 7.4 kW (single-phase) or 11–22 kW (three-phase), depending on the installation.
Protection rating: IP65/IP66 for outdoor and car-park use (dust and water resistance).
OCPP compatibility: for installations that need remote management, monitoring and per-use billing.
Load management (DLM) support: to share power evenly if more than one point is to be installed.

body.text: Bemis manufactures its domestically produced AC wallbox models at its facility in Bursa. The product range includes models in the 7.4–22 kW AC range with Type 2 connectors, IP65/IP66 protection and OCPP compatibility, along with CCS2-connector DC fast-charging solutions for road/fleet use. The devices carry the CE mark. You can decide which model suits which installation together with the qualified team, based on your vehicle's power, your installation and your usage scenario.

body.alt: Comparison of Mode 2 and Mode 3 AC charging: with Mode 2 the vehicle charges portably from a standard socket through an IC-CPD protection unit integrated into the cable, and it is slow because the power is limited by the socket; with Mode 3 the vehicle charges from a fixed wallbox with continuous communication at higher power and greater safety.
body.caption: The difference between Mode 2 (portable, IC-CPD protected, plug into a socket) and Mode 3 (fixed wallbox, continuous communication) AC charging.

body.text: How does load management work across multiple charging points?

In installations where several vehicles can charge at once — a building, a business or a fleet — what often falls short is not the device but the building's electrical capacity. If every point draws full power at the same time, the main fuse may trip or the grid may be strained. Load management (DLM – Dynamic Load Management) shares the available power intelligently among the points, keeping total consumption from exceeding the facility's safe limit. When only one vehicle is connected it receives more power; as a second and third vehicle are added, the system automatically redistributes power in a balanced way.

This makes it possible to offer charging at more points using the existing infrastructure, without an expensive subscription power upgrade or a new transformer. OCPP-compatible devices let you handle this management remotely through central software and bill each user's consumption separately. If you'd like to explore how load management works in detail, take a look at our dedicated guide on the subject.
Learn in detail how static and dynamic load balancing work.
body.label: Explore Load Management

body.alt: Dynamic load management (DLM) diagram: a 22 kW total power limit at the main panel is distributed to three wallboxes through a DLM controller. When only one vehicle is connected, almost all the power goes to that device; when three vehicles charge at once, the power is shared evenly and the total facility limit is not exceeded.
body.caption: DLM (dynamic load management): the main panel's total power is shared intelligently among the devices, and the main fuse doesn't trip.

body.text: What are the installation steps?

Once the permits and plan are ready, the physical installation usually takes little time. A typical installation proceeds in this order: a qualified electrician surveys the site and determines the mounting point; a separate supply line is run from the panel to the device; residual current and overcurrent protection is added to the panel; the device is fixed to the wall or a stand and wired; earthing is connected. Finally the device is powered up and tested, and if required registered with the OCPP/management software.

body.caption: Points to consider by installation location
rows: Separate line + RCD; usually no additional permit; 7.4 kW typical if single-phase.
Property owners' decision; separation of consumption from the shared line (separate meter / RFID); IP65–66; load management across multiple points.
Billing via OCPP; load management; grid power upgrade if required; outdoor protection.

body.text: Who should install and commission the charging station?

Installing a charging station is work that involves the electrical installation and carries continuous high current; for that reason it must always be carried out by a qualified electrician or authorised service. An unauthorised or careless installation carries the risk of fire, electric shock and device failure, and may also affect warranty coverage. A qualified installation guarantees that every detail — from correctly calculating the cable cross-section to properly selecting the protection devices — is done in line with the standards.

Once installation is complete, the device is commissioned and tested: it's confirmed that the protection devices work correctly, that the earthing is solid and that the device charges smoothly at the specified power. In an OCPP-compatible installation, the device is registered with the management software and prepared for remote monitoring and billing. Because this commissioning step confirms that everything works safely and correctly before the first charge, it's the final link that should never be skipped.

Whether your installation is for a home, a building or a business, with the right device selection and a qualified installation you can charge trouble-free for years. From the guides below you can explore the one that best fits your own scenario, and take a look at Bemis's OCPP-compatible, domestically produced models.
Explore Bemis's OCPP-compatible solutions for homes, buildings and businesses.

faq.q: Do you need a permit to install an EV charging station?
faq.a: It depends on the installation location. If you're installing in the garage of your own detached house, you generally won't need any additional permit — the decision is yours. If you're installing in a shared space such as an apartment or building car park, you first need a decision from the building management or property owners, because additional wiring is involved in a common area. In addition, for high-power or multi-point installations, total demand may exceed the existing subscription, so a power upgrade or grid opinion from the electricity distribution company may be required. While the regulations in Turkey are evolving to make charging infrastructure easier, the best approach to clarify the current situation is to speak with your building management and a qualified electrician.

faq.q: Is a separate electrical line essential for a charging station?
faq.a: Yes, for a sound installation the charging device should be fed as far as possible from a dedicated line run from the electrical panel. This line forms its own circuit at the panel with a device-specific fuse and residual current protection; that way there's no conflict with the home's other loads during charging and safety improves. Because a charging device draws high, continuous current over long periods, a standard socket circuit is not suitable for carrying this load safely. The cable cross-section of the dedicated line must be calculated correctly by a qualified electrician based on the device's power, whether it's single- or three-phase, and the distance between the panel and the device. This is the foundation of a charging experience that is both safe and efficient.

faq.q: How is the cable cross-section for a charging station determined?
faq.a: Cable cross-section determines the current a cable can carry safely without overheating and is one of the most critical technical factors in a charging installation. The correct cross-section is calculated according to the device's power — that is, its ampere rating — whether the installation is single- or three-phase, and the distance between the panel and the device. As distance increases, a thicker cable is usually needed to compensate for voltage drop. A cable with an inadequate cross-section overheats under continuous load, leading to efficiency loss and a safety risk. For this reason, rather than choosing a cable by guesswork, the precise calculation should be done by a qualified electrician. A correctly sized cable ensures the device operates at full performance and safely.

faq.q: What power and protection rating are suitable for a home charging device?
faq.a: Power is chosen according to the value your vehicle accepts and your installation's capacity. On single-phase installations the typical ceiling is 7.4 kW, while a three-phase connection allows faster charging in the 11–22 kW range. A device more powerful than needed provides no extra benefit if your vehicle can't draw that power. In terms of protection rating, devices rated IP65 or IP66 should be preferred for outdoor spaces such as open or semi-open car parks; this rating protects the device against dust and water. Bemis's IP65/IP66-protected, Type 2-connector models in the 7.4–22 kW range are built with this kind of use in mind. Choosing the right power and protection matters for long service life.

faq.q: Why is load management needed when installing multiple charging points?
faq.a: In installations where several vehicles can charge at once — a building, a business or a fleet — if all points draw full power the building's electrical capacity may be exceeded and the main fuse may trip. Load management (DLM) shares the available power intelligently among the points, keeping total consumption below the safe limit. When only one vehicle is connected it receives more power; as new vehicles are added, the system automatically redistributes power in a balanced way. This makes it possible to offer charging at more points using the existing infrastructure, without an expensive subscription upgrade or a new transformer. OCPP-compatible devices let you handle this management remotely and bill each user's consumption separately.

faq.q: Who should install and commission the charging station?
faq.a: Installing a charging station is work that involves the electrical installation and carries continuous high current; for that reason it must always be carried out by a qualified electrician or authorised service. An unauthorised installation carries the risk of fire, electric shock and device failure, and may also affect warranty coverage. A qualified installation guarantees that every detail — from correctly calculating the cable cross-section to selecting the protection devices — complies with the standards. Once installation is complete, the device is commissioned and tested: it's confirmed that the protection devices work, that the earthing is solid and that the device charges smoothly at the specified power. In an OCPP-compatible installation, the device is also registered with the management software and prepared for remote monitoring.

elektrikli-arac-sarj-terimleri-sozlugu.title: EV Charging Terminology Glossary
elektrikli-arac-sarj-terimleri-sozlugu.description: Every essential EV charging term in one place: AC/DC, Type 2, CCS2, kW/kWh, Mode 2/Mode 3, OCPP, V2L, load management and more.
elektrikli-arac-sarj-terimleri-sozlugu.excerpt: We've gathered the terms you need to understand EV charging with clear, concise definitions, grouped by topic: current types, connectors, power units, smart charging protocols and safety ratings.

body.text: The electric vehicle world has a vocabulary all its own: AC or DC, Type 2 or CCS2, are kW and kWh the same thing? This glossary brings together the terms you'll most often encounter in EV charging with short, clear, no-nonsense definitions. We've grouped the terms by topic so you can quickly find the concept you're looking for.
AC & DC Basics
AC Charging

In AC (alternating current) charging, converting the current into the direct current (DC) the battery needs is done by the charger built into the vehicle. It's suitable for home and workplace use; it's slow to medium speed (typically 7.4–22 kW) and, in Turkey, uses the Type 2 connector.
DC Charging

In DC (direct current) charging, the conversion is done inside the station and high power is delivered straight to the battery. It's fast charging (50–350+ kW), usually found at public points, and in Turkey uses the CCS2 connector.
Onboard Charger
The unit inside the vehicle that converts AC to DC, and it caps the vehicle's AC charging speed. Most vehicles charge at a maximum of 11 kW AC; some models support 7.4 kW or 22 kW.
Connectors & Cables
Type 1 (SAE J1772)
A single-phase AC charging connector, focused on North America and Japan. It's not widely used in Turkey.
Type 2 (Mennekes, IEC 62196-2)
The AC charging standard for Europe and Turkey. It supports both single-phase and three-phase charging.
CCS2 (Combined Charging System / Combo 2)
The Type 2 connector with two DC pins added beneath it. It's the DC fast-charging standard for Europe and Turkey.
CHAdeMO
A DC fast-charging standard of Japanese origin. Its use in Europe is steadily declining.
GB/T
China's charging standard, which uses separate connectors for AC and DC.
Mode 2
A portable charging cable that plugs into a socket and has a control box called an IC-CPD on it. It operates at low to medium power.
Mode 3
A cable connected to a fixed charging station (wallbox). It provides safer charging at higher power than Mode 2.
Power & Speed
kW (Kilowatt)
Expresses power — that is, the instantaneous charging speed. It shows how quickly the device is delivering energy to the battery at that moment.
kWh (Kilowatt-hour)
Expresses energy; it indicates battery capacity or the amount of electricity delivered to the vehicle. Roughly, charging time = kWh ÷ kW.
Single-Phase
A single-phase electrical connection that typically provides up to 7.4 kW in AC charging.
Three-Phase
A three-phase electrical connection that can provide 11 kW or 22 kW in AC charging.
Wallbox
A wall-mounted AC charging station. It's designed for home and workplace use.
SoC (State of Charge)
The battery's current charge percentage.
Taper
The marked slowdown in charging speed on DC fast charging after the battery passes 80%. It's applied to protect the battery.
Energy Direction: V2L, C2L, V2G
V2L (Vehicle-to-Load)
A feature that lets the vehicle battery supply electricity to external devices or to the home.
C2L (Charger-to-Load)
Provides electricity transfer much like V2L; this transfer takes place through the charging device.
V2G (Vehicle-to-Grid)
Feeding electricity from the vehicle battery back into the power grid.
Smart Charging (OCPP, etc.)
OCPP (Open Charge Point Protocol)
The open communication protocol between a charging device and a central management system. It enables functions such as remote monitoring, load management and per-user billing.
CSMS (Charging Station Management System)
The central software that manages charging points remotely.
Load Management (Load Balancing / Dynamic Load Balancing)
A method of sharing the available electrical capacity among devices. It allows several vehicles to charge without exceeding the installation's capacity.
RFID / NFC
A method of authorising a charging session by card or contactless reading.
Protection & Safety
IP65 / IP66
Indicates the device's protection rating against dust and water. These ratings denote suitability for outdoor use.
A quick reminder: kW is the speed of charging, while kWh is the amount of energy delivered. You can roughly find the duration by dividing kWh by kW.

Bemis E-V Charge is the Bursa-based domestic EV charging brand of Bemis Teknik Elektrik A.Ş., a manufacturer since 1994. You can see how the concepts in this glossary translate into real products across the AC Wallbox (7.4–22 kW), Type 2 cable (Mode 2 and Mode 3), V2L/C2L and CCS2 DC unit product families; all are CE, IP65-66 and OCPP compliant.
To see how these terms translate into real products, take a look at the Bemis E-V Charge product family.

faq.q: What is Type 2?
faq.a: Type 2 (Mennekes, IEC 62196-2) is the connector type that is the AC charging standard for Europe and Turkey. Its most important feature is that it supports both single-phase and three-phase charging; this allows it to be used at different power levels from 7.4 kW up to 22 kW, depending on your installation. In Turkey, this is the standard connector you'll come across in home and workplace AC charging, and it's used on wall-mounted AC charging stations (wallboxes) and on Type 2 cables. In other words, Type 2 is the connector you'll deal with most often in day-to-day charging. In addition, CCS2, the DC fast-charging standard, is built on top of Type 2, with two DC pins added beneath this connector.

faq.q: What does OCPP do?
faq.a: OCPP (Open Charge Point Protocol) is the open communication protocol between a charging device and a central management system (CSMS). A CSMS is the central software that manages charging points remotely. The fact that the protocol is open allows devices from different manufacturers to speak a common language. Thanks to it, functions such as remote monitoring, load management and per-user billing become possible; that is, you can track a charging point remotely, share the available capacity among devices, and measure who charged how much. It can also be used together with RFID/NFC card authorisation. These features become especially important in workplace, building and fleet installations where several devices are managed.

faq.q: What is the difference between Mode 2 and Mode 3?
faq.a: Mode 2 is a portable charging cable that plugs into a standard socket and has a control box called an IC-CPD on it; it operates at low to medium power and, thanks to its flexibility, is handy for emergency or temporary charging. Mode 3 is a cable connected to a fixed charging station (wallbox). Mode 3 provides charging that is both safer and at higher power than Mode 2; this is why the preferred method for regular, permanent use at home or work is Mode 3. In short, Mode 2 suits portability, while Mode 3 suits safe, fast fixed charging.

faq.q: What is the difference between kW and kWh?
faq.a: kW (kilowatt) expresses power — that is, the instantaneous charging speed; it shows how quickly the device is delivering energy to the battery at that moment. kWh (kilowatt-hour) expresses energy; it indicates battery capacity or the amount of electricity delivered to the vehicle. You can tell them apart like this: kW is like the flow rate of a tap, while kWh is like the total amount of water that fills up after the flow. From this relationship you can also roughly calculate charging time: the duration is found approximately by dividing the energy to be delivered (kWh) by the charging power (kW). For example, dividing 22 kWh of energy by 11 kW of power gives a charging time of roughly 2 hours; this is why it's important not to confuse these two units.

faq.q: What is the difference between AC and DC charging?
faq.a: In AC (alternating current) charging, converting the current into the direct current (DC) the battery needs is done by the vehicle's onboard charger. This onboard unit also caps the AC charging speed. That's why AC charging is generally slow to medium speed (7.4–22 kW), is suitable for home and workplace, and in Turkey uses the Type 2 connector. In DC (direct current) charging, the conversion is done inside the station and high power is delivered straight to the battery; that means fast charging (50–350+ kW). DC is usually found at public points and, in Turkey, uses the CCS2 connector.

faq.q: What is CCS2?
faq.a: CCS2 (Combined Charging System / Combo 2) is the Type 2 connector with two DC pins added beneath it, and it is the DC fast-charging standard for Europe and Turkey. Thanks to this design, the same connector area can house both AC and DC connections; in practice, many vehicles have Type 2 (AC) on top and CCS2 (DC) below together. CCS2 should be thought of not as a rival to Type 2 but as its extended version for DC. Because the conversion is done inside the station in DC charging, high power is delivered straight to the battery. When taking a high-power charge at a public fast-charging station in Turkey, the connector you'll come across will most likely be CCS2.

faq.q: What does V2L mean?
faq.a: V2L (Vehicle-to-Load) is the feature that lets the vehicle battery supply electricity to external devices or to the home; in other words, it lets you use your vehicle as a kind of portable power source. This is one of the solutions where the direction of energy flows outward from the vehicle. Working on a similar logic, C2L (Charger-to-Load) provides the same kind of electricity transfer through the charging device. A more advanced concept, V2G (Vehicle-to-Grid), is feeding electricity from the vehicle battery straight back into the power grid. So while V2L and C2L send energy outward from the vehicle, in V2G that energy is returned to the grid. In short, V2L is a practical feature that opens up the vehicle's energy for everyday use.

elektrikli-arac-sarj-suresi-kac-saatte-d.title: EV Charging Time: How Many Hours to Full? (AC and DC)
elektrikli-arac-sarj-suresi-kac-saatte-d.description: How many hours does an electric vehicle take to charge? Calculate AC and DC charging times with a simple formula, see example scenarios, and learn about the vehicle's accepted power limit.
elektrikli-arac-sarj-suresi-kac-saatte-d.excerpt: EV charging time depends fundamentally on battery capacity and charging power. We explain how to calculate the time for AC and DC with a simple formula, and why the vehicle's accepted power limit is the deciding factor, with worked examples.

body.text: The most common question before buying an electric vehicle is: "How many hours does it take to charge?" The answer isn't a single figure; it depends on the size of the battery, the power of the charging device and, most importantly, the maximum power the vehicle can accept. In this guide we give you a simple formula you can use to work out the time yourself, and share worked examples for AC (slow/normal) and DC (fast) charging.
The basic charging-time formula
You can roughly find the charging time with a single division. You divide the energy to be charged (kWh) by the charging power (kW):
Time (hours) ≈ Energy to be charged (kWh) ÷ Charging power (kW)

In real life there are heat and conversion losses during charging. That's why adding roughly 10–20% to the formula's result gives a more accurate estimate. For example, dividing 55 kWh of energy by 11 kW gives 5 hours; with losses included, in practice you should reckon on around 5.5 hours.

A point to note: the "energy to be charged" is not the whole battery but only the portion you want to fill. If you're going from 10% to 100%, you'll deliver about 54 kWh into a 60 kWh battery; if you start from 30%, that figure drops much lower.
AC (slow/normal) charging times
AC charging, used at home and at work, runs on the Type 2 connector in Turkey. The common power levels are:

items: Single-phase 7.4 kW (32A) — the most suitable option for a standard home installation
Three-phase 11 kW (16A) — the power most modern EVs support
Three-phase 22 kW (32A) — the fastest AC option (if the vehicle supports it)

body.text: Worked example: 60 kWh battery, from 10% to 100%

items: With a 7.4 kW wallbox ≈ 8 hours (ideal for an overnight charge)
With an 11 kW wallbox ≈ 5.5 hours
With a 22 kW wallbox ≈ 3 hours (if the vehicle accepts 22 kW AC)

body.text: IMPORTANT: The vehicle's accepted power limit is the deciding factor

No matter how powerful your charging device is, the vehicle isn't obliged to accept all of that power. On the AC side, the vehicle's "onboard charger" caps the speed. Many electric vehicles accept a maximum of 11 kW AC; some are limited to 7.4 kW, others to 22 kW.

Even if you buy a 22 kW wallbox, if your vehicle accepts only 11 kW the charge will proceed at 11 kW. In other words, the deciding factor is the lower of the two values — the charging device and the vehicle.

The same limit applies on the DC side: whatever the vehicle's "DC peak power" is, a more powerful fast-charging station can't exceed that speed. That's why the best approach before choosing a device is to find out both your vehicle's AC onboard and DC peak power.
DC (fast) charging times

DC fast charging is used at public stations with the CCS2 connector in Turkey and is generally preferred for long journeys. Typical power levels are 50 kW, 150 kW, 350 kW. There's a reason DC times are almost always given as from 10% to 80%: once the battery passes 80% the charging curve slows down (taper) and the final 20% takes disproportionately longer.
Worked example: 60 kWh battery, from 10% to 80%

items: With 50 kW DC ≈ 45–60 minutes
With 150 kW DC ≈ 20–30 minutes (if the vehicle accepts this power)
The portion from 80% to 100% takes disproportionately longer; on a long journey it usually makes more sense to stop at 80% and carry on

body.text: On DC too, the vehicle's DC peak power is the deciding factor. Even if you connect to a 150 kW station, if your vehicle accepts a maximum of 100 kW the charge is limited to that speed.
Factors that affect charging time

items: Battery capacity (kWh) — a bigger battery takes longer
Charging power (kW) — the power the device provides
The maximum power the vehicle accepts (AC onboard + DC peak) — this is often the real limit
Starting charge percentage — starting from 30% takes far less time than from 0%
Temperature — cold weather can slow charging
The DC charging curve (taper) — the slowdown after 80%
The installation — single-phase or three-phase

body.text: Practical tip: AC for daily use, DC for long journeys

Most drivers charge the battery not from 0% each day but from a level like 30–40%. That's why real daily charging time is far shorter than the full-charge times above. For daily use, an AC wallbox at home or work (which charges comfortably overnight) is generally sufficient; for long-journey needs, DC fast-charging stations along the route come into play.

Bemis E-V Charge, as the domestic EV charging brand of Bemis Teknik Elektrik A.Ş. (a manufacturer since 1994), produces AC wallboxes in the 7.4–22 kW range, Type 2 cables, portable AC charging solutions and a CCS2 DC fast-charging unit (e.g. the 40 kW BEVDC) in Bursa. The products are CE, IP65-66 and OCPP compliant. Keeping your vehicle's accepted power in mind when choosing the right device stops you paying for more power than you need.
Explore AC wallbox models for use at home or work.

faq.q: How many hours does an electric vehicle take to charge?
faq.a: There's no single figure; the time depends on the size of the battery, the charging power and, most importantly, the maximum power the vehicle can accept. For a rough calculation, divide the energy to be charged (kWh) by the charging power (kW), then add about 10–20% for heat and conversion losses. For example, filling a 60 kWh battery from 10% to 100% takes roughly 8 hours with 7.4 kW, about 5.5 hours with 11 kW, and about 3 hours with 22 kW (if the vehicle accepts that power). Remember, the energy you deliver is not the whole battery but only the portion you want to fill; if you start from 30%, the time is far shorter.

faq.q: How long does it take to charge a vehicle at 11 kW?
faq.a: Filling a 60 kWh battery from 10% to 100% at 11 kW AC takes roughly 5.5 hours, losses included. This is the most common scenario in home charging, because most modern electric vehicles can accept 11 kW AC. 11 kW generally requires a three-phase installation. In real life this time is often even shorter, because drivers usually top up the battery not from 0% but from a level like 30–40%. So an 11 kW wallbox is a practical daily charging solution that will comfortably fill the vehicle overnight.

faq.q: I bought a 22 kW wallbox but my vehicle charges more slowly — why?
faq.a: The reason is that the AC charging speed is capped by the charger inside the vehicle (the onboard charger). No matter how powerful your charging device is, the vehicle isn't obliged to accept all of that power. Many electric vehicles accept a maximum of 11 kW AC; some are limited to 7.4 kW. So if your vehicle accepts 11 kW, the charge takes place at 11 kW even if you connect a 22 kW wallbox. The deciding factor is the lower of the two values — the charging device and the vehicle. That's why the best approach before buying a device is to find out your vehicle's AC accepted power.

faq.q: How many minutes does DC fast charging take?
faq.a: For a 60 kWh battery, charging from 10% to 80% takes roughly 45–60 minutes with 50 kW DC and about 20–30 minutes with 150 kW DC (if the vehicle accepts that power). There's a reason DC times are almost always given up to 80%: once the battery passes 80% the charging curve slows down (taper) and the final 20% takes disproportionately longer. Also, as with AC, the vehicle's DC peak power is the deciding factor on DC; even if you connect to a 150 kW station, if your vehicle accepts a maximum of 100 kW the charge is limited to that speed.

faq.q: Why is DC charging usually given up to 80%?
faq.a: Because, to protect the battery, the charging curve slows down markedly after 80%; this is called taper. Because of this slowdown, the final stretch from 80% to 100% takes disproportionately longer than the first 80%. As a result, DC worked examples are almost always given from 10% to 80%. The practical upshot is this: on a long journey, waiting a long time at the station to top the vehicle up to 100% is usually not efficient; stopping at 80% and carrying on saves time and avoids tying up the station unnecessarily. A full daily charge is done more at home with AC.

faq.q: In daily use, is the vehicle charged from empty every day?
faq.a: No. Most drivers top up the battery not from 0% each day but from a level like 30–40%. That's why real daily charging time is far shorter than the full-charge times in the guides, because the energy you need to add (kWh) is far less. The higher the starting charge percentage, the shorter the time; starting from 30% finishes far faster than starting from 0%. In practice, an AC wallbox at home or work comfortably completes this partial charge while the vehicle is parked overnight. So in daily use there's no obligation to "fill from empty"; topping up as much as you've used overnight is enough, and this is done smoothly with AC.

faq.q: Should I install AC or DC fast charging at home?
faq.a: For daily use, an AC wallbox (7.4–22 kW) at home or work is generally sufficient; the vehicle charges comfortably overnight and most of the daily need is covered this way. Because most drivers already top up the battery not from 0% but from a level like 30–40%, the real daily time is short. DC fast charging, on the other hand, is more useful on long journeys, at public stations along the route. Keeping your vehicle's accepted power in mind when choosing the right device is important; this stops you paying for more power than you need. In short: daily charging is handled at home with AC, and long-journey needs with DC stations along the route; the two complement each other.

ev-sarj-soketi-tipleri-type-2-ccs2-chade.title: EV Charging Connector Types: The Difference Between Type 2, CCS2 and CHAdeMO
ev-sarj-soketi-tipleri-type-2-ccs2-chade.description: What is the difference between Type 2, CCS2 and CHAdeMO connectors? We compare AC and DC charging connectors and explain clearly which standard is used in Turkey.
ev-sarj-soketi-tipleri-type-2-ccs2-chade.excerpt: EV charging connectors can be confusing: what do Type 2, CCS2 and CHAdeMO mean? We define each one, compare their differences clearly, and explain which applies in Turkey and which connector to use at home versus on long journeys.

body.text: For newcomers to the electric vehicle (EV) world, one of the most confusing topics is charging connectors. Names like Type 2, CCS2, CHAdeMO and GB/T come up often, but which one does what is frequently unclear. In this article we define the most common charging connector types one by one, compare the differences between them, and explain in particular which standard applies in Turkey.

The basic distinction is this: some connectors are for AC (alternating current) charging, others for DC (direct current) fast charging. At home and at work you usually charge at slow to medium speed with AC; on long journeys you take a high-power charge in minutes at public DC stations. Connector types are largely shaped by this AC/DC distinction.
What is Type 1 (SAE J1772)?

Type 1 is a single-phase AC charging connector based on the SAE J1772 standard. It offers power in roughly the 3.7–7.4 kW range. It's seen more in North American, Japanese and some older Asian-made electric vehicles. It's not common in Europe and Turkey; in these markets the AC connector of the vehicles sold is almost always Type 2.
What is Type 2 (Mennekes)?

Type 2 (Mennekes, IEC 62196-2) is the AC charging standard for Europe and Turkey. It supports both single-phase and three-phase charging. The common power range in home and workplace AC charging is 7.4–22 kW (rarely reaching up to 43 kW AC). The AC charging connector of electric vehicles sold in Turkey is almost always Type 2, so when it comes to home charging, the connector you'll deal with is most likely this one.
What is CCS2 (Combo 2)?

CCS2 (Combined Charging System / Combo 2) is the Type 2 connector with two DC pins added beneath it, and it's for DC fast charging. It's the DC standard for Europe and Turkey. The typical power range starts at 50 kW and rises to 350 kW and above. An important point: on the same vehicle, Type 2 (AC) on top and CCS2 (DC) below are usually present together. In other words, CCS2 is not a rival to Type 2 but its DC-enabled, enlarged version.

body.alt: Comparison of the pin layout of Type 2 and CCS2 connectors: Type 2 has seven pins (L1, L2, L3 power + N neutral + PE earth + CP and PP communication) and provides only AC charging; CCS2 has the same seven pins plus two large DC pins (DC+ and DC−) beneath them, supporting both AC and DC fast charging in a single connector.
body.caption: The difference between Type 2 (AC only, 7 pins) and CCS2/Combo 2 (the same 7 pins + 2 DC pins) — with CCS2 you do both AC and DC fast charging through the same connector.

body.text: What is CHAdeMO?

CHAdeMO is a DC fast-charging standard of Japanese origin. It was common on some vehicles such as the older Nissan Leaf. However, its use in Europe is steadily declining and being phased out; the new generation of vehicles has largely moved to CCS2. In Turkey the CHAdeMO connector is rarely seen.
What is GB/T?

GB/T is China's national charging standard and uses separate connectors for AC and DC. You may come across it on some Chinese-made electric vehicles. It's not the main standard of the European and Turkish markets.
The difference between Type 2, CCS2 and CHAdeMO: a quick comparison
When we place the three main connectors side by side with their basic features, the difference becomes clear:

items: Type 2 (Mennekes): AC charging. Single-/three-phase. Common power 7.4–22 kW. The AC standard for Europe and Turkey. The connector of home and workplace charging.
CCS2 (Combo 2): DC fast charging. The Type 2 connector with 2 DC pins added beneath it. Typically 50–350+ kW. The DC standard for Europe and Turkey. The connector of public fast charging.
CHAdeMO: DC fast charging. Japanese standard. Was common on older vehicles (e.g. the older Nissan Leaf). Declining/being phased out in Europe. Rare in Turkey.
Type 1 (J1772): Single-phase AC, ~3.7–7.4 kW. Focused on North America/Japan. Not common in Turkey.
GB/T: Chinese standard, separate AC and DC connectors. On some Chinese-made EVs.

body.text: In short, the distinction has two layers: first AC or DC (Type 2 = AC, CCS2 and CHAdeMO = DC), then which region's standard (Type 2/CCS2 = Europe-Turkey, CHAdeMO = Japan, GB/T = China).
Which charging connector is used in Turkey?

In Turkey the picture is quite clear: Type 2 dominates on the AC side and CCS2 on the DC side. In home and workplace AC charging you'll come across Type 2 cables and Type 2-connector wallboxes. At public DC fast-charging stations, the CCS2 connector is the standard. CHAdeMO is rare and steadily declining.

Tesla vehicles also comply with these standards: in Europe and Turkey they use Type 2 for AC and CCS2 for DC, and the European Supercharger network also runs over CCS2. So when you buy an EV in Turkey, you'll almost certainly come across a vehicle with Type 2 on top and CCS2 below.
Turkey in a nutshell: at home and at work, AC = Type 2; on long journeys, public DC = CCS2. CHAdeMO is rare and declining.
Practical tip: which connector in which situation?
Your charging habits are largely determined by your daily routine. For most drivers, the practical upshot is this:

items: Home and workplace (daily charging): AC with Type 2. The right product is a Type 2-connector AC wallbox or a Type 2 charging cable. This is enough for the vehicle to charge overnight.
Long journeys (fast charging): DC with CCS2. At public DC stations you take a high-power charge in minutes; these stations' cables are already fixed, so you don't need to bring your own.
When choosing your cable, check your vehicle's connector type and whether your home connection is single- or three-phase; this directly affects the power you'll get.

body.text: So you don't need to buy a separate DC unit for long journeys; that infrastructure is ready at public stations. Your real investment is the home/workplace AC solution that handles daily charging: a Type 2 wallbox of the right power and a suitable Type 2 cable.

body.text: The cost of a home electric vehicle charging station cannot be summed up in a single figure, because it depends on many factors — from the power of the device to the condition of your installation. In this guide, we explain the main headings that determine the price in plain language, and cover what you should keep in mind to plan your budget correctly. For a current price and quote, you can reach us through our product page.
1) The power of the device (kW)

Chargers typically range from 7.4 kW (single phase) to 22 kW (three phase). Higher power means faster charging, but it requires your installation to be three-phase. For most home users, 7.4–11 kW is more than sufficient for overnight charging; excessive power increases both device and infrastructure cost.
2) Tethered or socketed?

Fixed tethered models are practical — you plug in the cable and start charging. With socketed models, you carry the cable separately; this provides flexibility for different vehicles. Cable length and quality also affect the total cost.
3) Smart features (OCPP, app, load management)

A basic device only charges; a smart device offers app control, user identification (RFID), remote monitoring and load management via OCPP. In residential-complex and workplace installations, these features are required for user-based billing and determine the device class.
4) Protection class (IP65 / IP66)

For a device to be installed outdoors, a high protection class against dust and water (IP65/IP66) is essential. Cheap devices with low protection have a short service life outdoors and prove more expensive in the long run.
5) Installation and electrical infrastructure

Alongside the device price, factor in the installation item too: running cable from the panel to the device, a residual current device (RCD), a fuse, and panel reinforcement if needed. The distance of the car park from the panel and the condition of the existing installation are the factors that most affect the installation cost.
6) From the manufacturer or from a reseller?

Buying a device directly from its manufacturer lowers the cost by eliminating the import and reseller margins in between; you also avoid waiting for service and spare parts. Bemis E-V Charge is a domestic brand that produces everything from hardware to software at its facility in Bursa — which provides an advantage on both price and support.
So how much is the electricity expense?

The device is a one-time investment; the real recurring expense is the electricity spent on charging. You can find your approximate cost per km by multiplying the kWh your vehicle consumes per 100 km by the unit electricity price at home. Overnight charging at home is generally noticeably more economical than public DC fast charging.

faq.q: How much is a home charging station?
faq.a: The cost of a home charging station cannot be summed up in a single figure, because the price is determined by many factors together. Chief among them are the power of the device (7.4–22 kW), whether it is tethered or socketed, smart features such as OCPP/app/load management, the protection class (IP65/IP66), and the installation conditions. Whether you buy the device directly from the manufacturer or from a reseller also affects the cost. That is why, to plan the budget correctly, you need to clarify the features that suit your needs. For a current price and quote tailored to you, you can get in touch through our product page.

faq.q: Is charging at home or fast charging out and about cheaper?
faq.a: For daily use, AC charging done overnight at home is generally noticeably more economical than public DC fast charging. The device is a one-time investment; the real recurring expense is the electricity spent on charging. To find your approximate cost per km, you can multiply the kWh your vehicle consumes per 100 km by the unit electricity price at home. DC fast charging, on the other hand, is mainly ideal for long journeys; its speed is high, but it proves more expensive than slow charging at home in a daily routine. For this reason, the smartest approach is to use home charging for daily needs and fast charging on the road.

faq.q: How many kW device should I buy?
faq.a: Chargers typically range from 7.4 kW (single phase) to 22 kW (three phase). For most home users, 7.4–11 kW is more than sufficient for overnight charging; the car is full by morning. Faster charging is possible at 22 kW, but this requires your installation to be three-phase. Choosing more power than you need unnecessarily increases both the device and electrical infrastructure cost. That is why first assessing your daily charging need and whether your installation is single or three phase is the soundest way to choose the right, economical power rating.

faq.q: Apart from the device price, what does the installation cost depend on?
faq.a: Alongside the device price, you need to factor in the installation item too. The installation cost is determined by the cable to be run from the panel to the device, the residual current device (RCD), the fuse, and panel reinforcement if needed. Among these items, the factor that most affects the cost is the distance of the car park from the panel and the condition of the existing installation; the farther the panel is from the device and the more inadequate the installation, the more the installation cost rises. For an outdoor installation, an IP65/IP66 protection class device is also essential. For proper planning, assessing the device and installation cost together from the outset prevents budget surprises.

faq.q: Why is there a price difference between a smart charger and a basic device?
faq.a: A basic device only charges; a smart device, on the other hand, offers features such as app control, user identification (RFID), remote monitoring and load management via OCPP. These capabilities determine the class of the device and therefore its price. For a home user, a basic or mid-level device is often sufficient. In residential-complex and workplace installations, however, smart features are almost mandatory; because user-based billing, remote monitoring and load management that shares the existing electrical capacity are made possible by these features. Determining the need correctly prevents paying for features you do not need.

ioniq-5-v2l-nasil-kullanilir.title: How to Use V2L with the Ioniq 5? A V2L / C2L Adapter Guide
